chunks: "Clock frequency directly sets how often the circuit switches, so dynamic power is alpha C V squared f . At a fixed voltage, double the frequency and you double the dynamic power.
Performance goes up with frequency too, but not perfectly: only the part of the work that is limited by the core clock speeds up.
If the program spends time waiting on DRAM, which doesn't get faster when I raise the CPU clock, I get less than the full gain.
For example, if 30% of the time is memory-bound, 2x clock gives about 1. 54x speedup. The real cost is that you can't raise frequency for free.
Faster clocks mean shorter cycle times, so the logic needs a higher supply voltage to meet timing, and power goes with the square of the voltage.
So along a DVFS curve power grows much faster than frequency; if voltage scaled in proportion it would be frequency cubed, and in practice it lands in between.
For instance, 2 gigahertz at 0. 9 volts to 4 gigahertz at 1. 1 volts is 2x the frequency but about 3x the power. That power turns into heat.
Junction temperature is ambient plus power times thermal resistance, and leakage grows exponentially with temperature, so a hot chip burns more power, which makes it hotter.
That feedback can cause throttling or even runaway.
So the system uses frequency as the main control knob: boost when there is thermal headroom, throttle down when it's hot, and drop frequency and voltage together when load is light to save energy."
